title: Truly subquadratic exact Euclidean bipartite matching
formal: Does there exist a uniform algorithm and absolute constants \(\delta,C>0\) that, for every \(n\ge1\) and every pair of labelled planar point lists \(R=(r_1,\ldots,r_n)\), \(B=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)\), returns a permutation \(\pi\in S_n\) minimizing \(\sum_{i=1}^n\|r_i-b_{\pi(i)}\|_2\), using at most \(Cn^{2-\delta}\) operations in the real-arithmetic model below, with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input? Deterministic algorithms qualify. Coordinates are arbitrary real numbers and there is no separation, spread or grid promise.
definitions:
The input consists of the two explicit lists of coordinate pairs in \(\mathbb R^2\); coincident points remain distinct labelled objects. A feasible matching pairs each red label with exactly one blue label and conversely. Its edge length is \(\|(x,y)-(u,v)\|_2=\sqrt{(x-u)^2+(y-v)^2}\). The output is the list of matched labels, and any minimizer is acceptable when several matchings tie. Squared Euclidean lengths define a different objective.

The editorial computational convention is a uniform real RAM with exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero value, comparison and nonnegative square root, each costing one operation. Reading or writing one register, branching, and drawing a fair random bit also cost one. Integer registers are used for addressing and ordinary control; no operation extracts an arbitrarily long binary expansion of a real in one step. Input reals are accessed as atomic coordinates, so this is an arithmetic-operation question rather than a finite-bit encoding theorem. The program is finite and independent of the input size.

The stated operation bound is worst-case over inputs and random choices; success probability refers only to the algorithm's coins on each fixed input. A successful output must attain the exact minimum, not merely an approximation to its cost. This bounded-error convention explicitly resolves the imported draft's unspecified randomization convention. The exponent improvement and constant must be independent of all coordinates, including the ratio between largest and smallest nonzero distances. An estimate containing an uncontrolled coordinate-dependent factor does not meet the bound. No preprocessing of a supplied table of all red-blue distances is free: the given input has only \(4n\) real coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the displayed operation and success guarantees, or a Lean-checked refutation in this specified model. A positive answer includes exact optimality on the successful event and one fixed exponent improvement for every input. A negative answer must exclude every such algorithm and every positive fixed improvement, rather than exhibit a bad case for a particular method. Approximate matching, a guarantee only for random point sets, or a grid-dependent time bound does not establish the proposition.
context:
This is the exact, one-to-one bipartite optimization problem underlying equal-mass empirical transport. The SWAT 2022 paper defines the same matching objective but studies multiplicative approximation. Its introduction contrasts roughly quadratic exact planar algorithms with faster bounds under integer-coordinate assumptions.

The 2023 exact algorithm improves expected time for independently sampled point sets, with an additional spread dependence. Its stochastic-input guarantee does not supply a uniform subquadratic bound over arbitrary real-coordinate inputs.

The catalogue question did not fix a machine or error model. The explicit real-RAM and bounded-error conventions above are editorial choices, recorded to make the selected benchmark precise; the bibliography is not being cited as fixing these exact conventions.

import_provenance.original_title: Truly subquadratic exact Euclidean bipartite matching
import_provenance.original_statement: Given n red and n blue points with arbitrary real coordinates in the plane, can a minimum-total-Euclidean-length perfect red–blue matching be computed in O(n^{2-epsilon}) time for fixed epsilon>0? Near-linear approximation schemes do not settle exact optimization.

sentences: The input is two equally sized labelled sets of points in the Euclidean plane.
The task is to find an exactly minimum-length one-to-one red-blue matching in truly subquadratic time.
The card fixes a real-arithmetic model and permits bounded-error randomization on every fixed input.
Fast approximation and faster stochastic-input algorithms have different guarantees.
A solution would show whether planar geometry alone removes a polynomial part of the quadratic exact-optimization cost.
